rows.stem: The molar ionic conductivities of \(\mathrm{Al^{3+}}\) and \(\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}\) are 189 \(\mathrm{S\ cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\) and 160 \(\mathrm{S\ cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\) respectively. The value of limiting molar conductivity of \(\mathrm{Al_2(SO_4)_3}\) will be :
rows.solution:
By Kohlrausch's law the limiting molar conductivity is the sum of the contributions of ALL the ions the formula unit gives, each counted AS OFTEN AS IT APPEARS.

Aluminium sulphate gives TWO aluminium ions and THREE sulphate ions:
\(\Lambda_m^{\circ}(\mathrm{Al_2(SO_4)_3}) = 2\lambda^{\circ}_{\mathrm{Al^{3+}}} + 3\lambda^{\circ}_{\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}}\)
\(= 2(189) + 3(160) = 378 + 480\)

\(\Lambda_m^{\circ} = 858\ \mathrm{S\ cm^2\ mol^{-1}}\)

The two multipliers are the whole question. Adding the figures once gives 349, and swapping them — three aluminiums and two sulphates — gives 887; neither is offered, but the distractors are built the same way.

Read the multipliers off the FORMULA, not off the charges: the subscripts 2 and 3 say how many of each ion the unit releases, and those are what the law counts.

rows.subtopic: Temperature Dependence of the Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem: The fraction of molecules having energy equal to or greater than activation energy is :
rows.solution:
The fraction of molecules with energy equal to or greater than the activation energy is \(e^{-E_a/RT}\).

It comes from the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution of molecular energies, and the FORM tells its own story. The exponent is NEGATIVE, so the value is always less than 1 — as it must be, being a fraction. Raise the temperature and \(E_a/RT\) shrinks, the exponent moves towards zero and the fraction RISES, which is why reactions go faster when heated.

The other options are the neighbouring pieces of the Arrhenius equation, \(k = Ae^{-E_a/RT}\). \(A\) is the FREQUENCY FACTOR, counting collisions of the right orientation; \(k\) is the rate constant itself; and \(Ae^{-E_a/RT}\) is their product, which IS \(k\).

Only the exponential term alone is the fraction.

rows.stem: Identify the primary amine from the given options :
rows.solution:
The primary amine is ETHYLAMINE, \(\mathrm{C_2H_5NH_2}\).

An amine is classified by how many CARBON GROUPS are attached to its nitrogen. Ethylamine's nitrogen carries ONE ethyl group and TWO hydrogens, which makes it primary.

Of the others, \((\mathrm{C_2H_5})_2\mathrm{NH}\) has two carbon groups and one hydrogen, so it is SECONDARY; both \((\mathrm{C_2H_5})_3\mathrm{N}\) and \((\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{N}\) have three carbon groups and no hydrogen at all, so they are TERTIARY.

The count of nitrogen-hydrogen bonds is what the classification really tracks, and it is what decides how each behaves with Hinsberg's reagent — two hydrogens give an alkali-soluble product, one gives an insoluble one, and none gives no reaction.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Phenols are stronger acids than alcohols.
Reason (R) : Alkoxide ion is more stable than phenoxide ion.
rows.context: For questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given – one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
The Assertion is TRUE, but the Reason is FALSE.

Phenols ARE stronger acids than alcohols — \(\mathrm{pK_a}\) about 10 against about 16, six orders of magnitude.

But the Reason has the stability the wrong way round. It is the PHENOXIDE ion that is the more stable, not the alkoxide. In phenoxide the negative charge is delocalised INTO THE BENZENE RING by resonance, spread over the ortho and para carbons as well as the oxygen. An alkoxide has no such escape: its charge sits entirely on one oxygen, and the alkyl group, being electron releasing, pushes still more density onto it.

And that is exactly why the Assertion holds. The more stable the anion, the more readily the parent gives up its proton — so a more stable PHENOXIDE means a MORE acidic phenol.

Corrected, the Reason would have explained the Assertion perfectly; as written it would predict the opposite.

rows.stem:
Define the following terms :
(a) Half life period (\(\mathrm{t_{1/2}}\))
(b) Effective collisions
rows.solution:
(a) HALF LIFE PERIOD, \(t_{1/2}\), is the time in which the concentration of a reactant is reduced to ONE HALF of its initial value.

What it depends on differs with the order, and that is what makes it diagnostic. For FIRST order \(t_{1/2} = 0{\cdot}693/k\), which carries no concentration term at all — the time to halve is the same whatever the reaction starts from. For ZERO order \(t_{1/2} = [\mathrm{A}]_0/2k\), directly proportional to the starting concentration; for SECOND order it is inversely proportional.

(b) EFFECTIVE COLLISIONS are those collisions which actually RESULT IN THE FORMATION OF PRODUCTS.

Most collisions do not. To be effective a collision must satisfy two conditions at once: the molecules must carry at least the THRESHOLD ENERGY, so that the existing bonds can be broken, and they must meet in the PROPER ORIENTATION, so that the atoms which are to bond are brought together.

The two requirements appear separately in the Arrhenius equation — the energy condition as \(e^{-E_a/RT}\) and the orientation condition inside the frequency factor \(A\).

rows.subtopic: Colligative Properties and Determination of Molar Mass
rows.stem: A solution containing 60 g of a non-volatile solute in 250 g of water freezes at 270.67 K. Calculate the molar mass of the solute. (\(\mathrm{K_f}\) of water = 1.86 K kg \(\mathrm{mol^{-1}}\)).
rows.solution:
The solution freezes at 270.67 K and pure water at 273.15 K, so the depression is
\(\Delta T_f = 273{\cdot}15 - 270{\cdot}67 = 2{\cdot}48\ \mathrm{K}\)

Combine the freezing point depression formula with the mass data:
\(\Delta T_f = \dfrac{K_f \times w_B \times 1000}{M_B \times w_A}\)

Rearranging for the molar mass, with \(w_B = 60\) g of solute and \(w_A = 250\) g of water:
\(M_B = \dfrac{K_f \times w_B \times 1000}{w_A \times \Delta T_f} = \dfrac{1{\cdot}86 \times 60 \times 1000}{250 \times 2{\cdot}48}\)
\(= \dfrac{111600}{620}\)

\(M_B = 180\ \mathrm{g\ mol^{-1}}\)

The answer is worth recognising: 180 g per mole is the molar mass of GLUCOSE, which is the commonest non-volatile solute in problems of this kind — a useful check that the arithmetic has landed somewhere sensible.

rows.stem:
Which of the following compounds will react more rapidly by \(\mathrm{S_N1}\) reaction and why ?
(a) \(\mathrm{CH_3-C(CH_3)_2-Br}\) or \(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2\,Br}\)
(b) Arrange the following compounds in the increasing order of their boiling points :
Bromoform, Dibromomethane, Chloromethane, Bromomethane
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE — part (a)'s first compound is drawn with real vertical bond lines to the two branch methyls rather than set inline, so the printed form is a small structure. The stem already carries it losslessly as a condensed formula, so the row is answerable from text alone; the crop is worth attaching only to show the paper's own layout. Page idx 10.
rows.solution:
(a) \((\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{C{-}Br}\), 2-bromo-2-methylpropane, reacts more rapidly.

The rate of an \(\mathrm{S_N}1\) reaction is set entirely by how easily the CARBOCATION forms, since that is the slow step — so the question is which cation is the more stable.

This compound is TERTIARY, and its cation is stabilised by electron release from THREE methyl groups. Bromoethane is PRIMARY, and its cation has only one such group to help it.

Note that the same bulk which favours \(\mathrm{S_N}1\) HINDERS \(\mathrm{S_N}2\), where the nucleophile must reach the carbon from behind — which is why the two orders run exactly opposite to each other.

(b) Increasing order of boiling point:
CHLOROMETHANE < BROMOMETHANE < DIBROMOMETHANE < BROMOFORM

Boiling point here tracks the MOLECULAR MASS, because van der Waals forces grow with the number of electrons a molecule has and how polarisable they are.

Chloromethane and bromomethane have one halogen each, and bromine is the heavier and more polarisable — so bromomethane boils higher. Adding a second bromine gives dibromomethane, and a third gives bromoform, each step adding mass and raising the boiling point further: 249 K, 277 K, 370 K and 423 K respectively.

rows.stem:
(a) What happens when Glucose reacts with Nitric acid ? Write chemical equation.
(b) Write one structural difference between DNA and RNA.
rows.solution:
(a) WITH NITRIC ACID — the concentrated acid, a strong oxidising agent — BOTH ends of the molecule are oxidised: the aldehyde at \(\mathrm{C_1}\) and the primary alcohol at \(\mathrm{C_6}\). The product is the dicarboxylic SACCHARIC ACID:
\(\mathrm{CHO(CHOH)_4CH_2OH} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{HNO_3}} \mathrm{COOH(CHOH)_4COOH}\)

The contrast with bromine water is the point. That MILDER reagent touches only the aldehyde and gives gluconic acid, a MONOcarboxylic acid — which is how the primary hydroxyl at the far end is established separately.

(b) DNA is DOUBLE stranded — two chains wound into a helix and held together by hydrogen bonds between complementary bases — whereas RNA is SINGLE stranded.

Two other structural differences serve equally well. The sugar differs: DNA has \(\beta\)-D-2-DEOXYRIBOSE, lacking the hydroxyl at \(\mathrm{C_2}\), while RNA has \(\beta\)-D-RIBOSE. And the fourth base differs: DNA carries THYMINE where RNA carries URACIL.

rows.stem:
(a) Draw the geometrical isomers of the given complex :
\(\mathrm{[Pt(NH_3)_2Cl_2]^{2+}}\)
(b) Write the electronic configuration of \(\mathrm{d^5}\) ion if \(\Delta_0 < \mathrm{P}\).
(c) What is an ambidentate ligand ?
rows.solution:
(a) The complex has two ammine ligands and two chlorido ligands around a single platinum, so the two chlorides may sit adjacent or opposite. In the square planar arrangement:

CIS ISOMER: the two chlorido ligands on ADJACENT corners of the square, with the two ammine ligands on the other two.

TRANS ISOMER: the two chlorido ligands on OPPOSITE corners, with the two ammines likewise opposite each other.

The pair is famous in medicine — cis-platin is an anticancer drug while the trans isomer is inactive, so the geometry is the whole of the difference. Note the charge as printed: two neutral ammines and two chlorido ligands giving \(-2\), against an overall \(+2\), puts platinum at \(+4\).

(b) \(\Delta_{\mathrm{o}} < \mathrm{P}\) means the splitting costs LESS than pairing, so electrons spread out singly over all five orbitals before any pair up. For \(d^5\):
\(t_{2g}^3\,e_g^2\)
with FIVE unpaired electrons — the maximum any d ion can have, and a HIGH SPIN complex. Had \(\Delta_{\mathrm{o}}\) exceeded \(\mathrm{P}\), the configuration would have been \(t_{2g}^5\,e_g^0\), low spin, with one.

(c) An AMBIDENTATE LIGAND is one with TWO DIFFERENT DONOR ATOMS, of which it binds the metal through only ONE AT A TIME.

The nitrite ion is the standard case: it may attach through its NITROGEN, as nitro, or through an OXYGEN, as nitrito. The thiocyanate ion behaves the same way, binding through sulphur or through nitrogen.

The choice gives rise to LINKAGE ISOMERISM, the two forms being genuinely different compounds with different colours. Note that ambidentate is not the same as BIDENTATE, which uses two atoms at once.

rows.stem:
Define the following terms :
(a) Glycosidic linkage
(b) Primary structure of protein
(c) Disaccharides
rows.solution:
(a) A GLYCOSIDIC LINKAGE is the OXIDE linkage joining two monosaccharide units, formed by the loss of a molecule of water between them.

It runs from the anomeric carbon of one sugar, through an oxygen, to a carbon of the next — \(\mathrm{C_1}\) to \(\mathrm{C_4}\) in maltose, for instance. It is what builds disaccharides and polysaccharides, and hydrolysing it is what breaks them back down.

(b) The PRIMARY STRUCTURE of a protein is the SPECIFIC SEQUENCE in which its amino acids are linked, through peptide bonds, along the chain.

It is the most fundamental level of protein structure, because all the higher levels follow from it: how the chain coils and folds is determined by which residues sit where. Denaturation destroys the secondary and tertiary structures while leaving the primary one intact, since no peptide bond is broken.

(c) DISACCHARIDES are carbohydrates that yield TWO molecules of monosaccharide on hydrolysis.

Sucrose gives glucose and fructose; maltose gives two glucose units; lactose gives glucose and galactose. The two units are joined by a glycosidic linkage, and whether the disaccharide is REDUCING depends on whether that linkage leaves an anomeric carbon free — maltose and lactose do, sucrose does not.

rows.stem:
(a) Write the IUPAC name of the given compound :
\(\mathrm{CH_2=CH-CH_2-CH_2-Cl}\)
(b) Why is thionyl chloride preferred for preparing alkyl halides from alcohols ?
(c) What happens when Methyl bromide reacts with KCN ?
rows.solution:
(a) The parent chain is four carbons with a double bond, so the compound is a BUTENE. Number from the end that gives the DOUBLE BOND the lower locant — the principal characteristic being the unsaturation, not the halogen — which puts the double bond between \(\mathrm{C_1}\) and \(\mathrm{C_2}\) and the chlorine on \(\mathrm{C_4}\):
4-CHLOROBUT-1-ENE

Numbering from the other end would have given the chlorine position 1 but the double bond position 3, which is the higher locant for the group that takes priority.

(b) Because both of its BY-PRODUCTS ARE GASES and escape from the reaction mixture:
\(\mathrm{R{-}OH} + \mathrm{SOCl_2} \longrightarrow \mathrm{R{-}Cl} + \mathrm{SO_2} + \mathrm{HCl}\)

Sulphur dioxide and hydrogen chloride both leave as gases, so the alkyl halide is obtained PURE and needs no separation. The reaction is also driven forwards by their escape.

The alternatives are messier. Phosphorus halides leave phosphorus-containing residues behind, and a halogen acid needs the products to be separated from water and unreacted acid. Thionyl chloride's advantage is entirely one of workup, which is why it is called the DARZEN'S procedure and preferred in the laboratory.

(c) SUBSTITUTION occurs, and the product is METHYL CYANIDE:
\(\mathrm{CH_3{-}Br} + \mathrm{KCN} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH_3CN} + \mathrm{KBr}\)

The product is also called ethanenitrile or acetonitrile, and note the CARBON COUNT: it has TWO carbons where the halide had one, the extra carbon coming from the cyanide ion.

The choice of metal cyanide matters. POTASSIUM cyanide is largely ionic in solution, so the free cyanide ion attacks through its CARBON — the better nucleophilic site — giving the nitrile. SILVER cyanide is mainly covalent, so attack occurs through the NITROGEN instead and the product is the ISOcyanide.
